issues.description: The release has no complete analysis dataset and omits the many distinct named raw/prepared files consumed by Section 2. The packaged workbook supplies only company/year identifiers. Input routes and exact coverage remain unverified; this is not evidence that access is denied.
Step 1.2 depends on manual duplicate-name checks and edits/copies across audit_EQR.xls Sheet2/Sheet3 before eqrcode is merged. The release contains no completed crosswalk workbook.

The code needs at least 2011-2014 data for prior_audit across target years 2013-2015, while dcosign and cumulative engagement histories use all earlier records without a coded start year. The supplied inputs and earliest available history are absent/unknown.

lowrank is referenced but never generated in the PDF. The ranking workbook is imported without a keep filter and may already contain it; its presence and values are unknown. Inspect the actual author workbook and preserve a valid field. If absent, only add the documented rank_cicpa>25 definition after confirming the input ranks/cutoff.

Table 4 Panel A uses shno, while share.xls imports keep only cpacode/auditor/yr/share and thereby drop the comment-documented shno field. The rank workbook is merged without a field restriction and may carry shno, but no firm-year source/key/definition is documented. Preserve any existing field and resolve its contract before changing code.

The supplied Stata program is embedded in a PDF with Windows D: roots rather than a standalone .do driver. It requires extraction/reflow and routine host-visible directory configuration before a later run; this is preparation, not evidence of a code incompatibility.

// We obtain the CPA code for each individual auditor from the Ministry of Finance
(MOF). We have maintained a database (titled as "audit_upto2015.xls") to store each
company-year observation (code, yr) with the audit firm (with the variable name

evidence.description: The program documents CICPA rank/revenue/CPA fields, imports the ranking workbook without a keep filter, and later uses lowrank.
evidence.quote:
*** Introduce audit firm ranking (CICPA rank)
// The CICPA ranks top 100 audit firms nationwide on its website (www.cicpa.org.cn)
every year. We compile the ranking data (with the variable name "rank_cicpa"), annual
total revenues (with the variable name "totrev"), and total number of CPAs (with the
variable name "cpano") for our sample period and stored in an excel file titled as
"rank_cicpa_2013to2015.xlsx".
// We identify large audit firms as those who ranked top-10 in each year during the
sample period (i.e., 2013-2015), thus ensuring the group of large vs. small audit firms to
be consistent across the period. Then we measure small firms in the sample (with the
variable name "ntop10", labeled as SMAUD in the paper).
// In untabulated analyses, we further differentiate between medium and small firms by
using the 25th ranking as the cutoff (with the variable name "lowrank" = 1 for audit firms
ranked lower than 25th [i.e., small-sized], and 0 for audit firms ranked higher than 25th
[i.e., medium-sized]).

preserve
cd $dir6
import excel using rank_cicpa_2013to2015.xlsx,first clear
replace audfirm=audfirm+"会计师事务所（特殊普通合伙）"
cd $dir0
save temp.dta,replace
restore
merge m:1 audfirm yr using temp.dta
drop _m

cap drop top10 ntop10
gen top10=(rank_cicpa<=8 | (rank_cicpa==9&yr==2013) | (rank_cicpa==10&yr==2014)
| (rank_cicpa==10&yr==2015)) if rank_cicpa!=. // To identify large audit firms as those
                         who consistently ranked top-10 in every year of the sample
                         period
gen ntop10=1-top10
cap drop medium small
gen medium=(ntop10==1 & lowrank!=1) if rank_cicpa!=.
gen small=(ntop10==1 & lowrank==1) if rank_cicpa!=.

save main.dta,replace

evidence.description: The appendix discusses additional quadratic and rank-transformed analyses.
evidence.quote:
3. Do the data suggest non-monotonic relationships between partner ownership and audit adjustments?

To determine whether the data support a non-monotonic relation, we estimate quadratic
specifications for our ownership variables. As shown in Table D, we generally find that the
quadratic terms are insignificant whereas the linear terms remain positive and significant for EQ
reviewer ownership. Therefore, we find little evidence to support a quadratic relationship. We
think this makes sense because the theoretical arguments for a non-monotonic relationship in the
corporate finance literature do not carry over in a straightforward fashion to the setting of audit
partner ownership. This additional analysis is reported in footnote 23 of the paper.

In another untabulated test, we also estimate cubic specifications for our ownership variables and
find that none of the cubic terms are statistically significant. An important limitation of the cubic
specifications, however, is that the variance-inflation-factors (VIFs) are very high. In the cubic
specifications, the VIFs for the ownership variables range from 48 to 295, implying that
multicollinearity is extremely high. In the quadratic specification, the variance-inflation-factors
(VIFs) for the ownership variables range from 16.5 to 21.9, which is high but not extremely high.



4. Are the results robust to using rank transformations?

Table E presents results using rank transformations for both the audit adjustment and ownership
variables.2 Our main results remain unchanged. Specifically, the coefficient on Rank(OWN_REV)

evidence.description: The appendix reports additional medium/small audit-firm comparisons beyond the supplied main-table program.
evidence.quote:
We also conduct an additional comparison of medium-sized and small audit firms (each firm’s
size ranking is shown in Panel B of Table I, with the cutoff between medium and small firms
being ranked 25th out of 40 audit firms).

Panel A of Table I shows that the mean (median) number of equity partners for large, medium-
sized, and small audit firms is 145 (115), 55 (49), and 36 (32), respectively. The mean and median
tests show that the differences in size are statistically significant. Although the differences in size
between the medium-sized and small firms are statistically significant, these differences are much
smaller than the differences between the Big 10 and medium-sized firms. This suggests that the
cleanest partition is between Big 10 and non-Big 10 rather than between medium-sized and small.
This is also consistent with prior China research in auditing which typically distinguishes
between the Big 10 and non-Big 10 audit firms.

Next, we examine whether the effects of ownership are significantly different between large,
medium-sized, and small audit firms. There are 2,794 audits conducted by large firms, 1,179
audits conducted by the medium-sized firms (MEDIUM = 1) and 757 audits conducted by the
small firms (SMALL = 1). We include interactions between MEDIUM (and SMALL) and our
ownership variables to test whether the effects of ownership are weaker at the medium-sized or
small audit firms. The results are reported in Table J. It shows that the coefficients on both
LnOWN_REV × MEDIUM and LnOWN_REV × SMALL are negative and statistically significant.
This suggests that the positive effects of EQ reviewer ownership are significantly attenuated at
both the medium-sized and small audit firms, relative to the Big 10 firms. The differences in the


                                                  6

coefficients between LnOWN_REV × MEDIUM and LnOWN_REV × SMALL are not statistically
significant. This suggests that the moderating effect of audit firm size is driven by differences
between Big 10 and non-Big 10 audit firms rather than differences between medium-sized and
small audit firms.
